newsitem.title: GERMANY: Pocket PCs take CeBIT stage before consumer crowds.
newsitem.headline: Pocket PCs take CeBIT stage before consumer crowds.

text.p: A horde of new handheld computers grabbed the spotlight at the CeBIT computer trade fair as consumers packed the aisles for the exposition's weekend sessions.
Philips Electronics NV, Hewlett-Packard Co, and Casio Computer Ltd were giving Europe its first glimpse of the "PC companions" that use a new version of Windows software.
Others showed off pint-sized computers showing pictures from digital cameras and tapping into the Internet via mobile phones.
The little machines were drawing even bigger crowds as CeBIT threw open its doors to online junkies, students and hobbyists after hosting a more staid business set since Thursday.

"We don't have enough demonstration units for all the people who want (to give) it a try," said a Hewlett-Packard staffer giving introductory lessons the company's OmniGo 300LX. "And it can be a long wait."

The OmniGo, the Philips Velo 1 and Casio's Cassiopeia are among the first of several 14-ounce palmtops using Windows CE, a slimmed-down version of Windows 95 that Microsoft Corp. produced for pocket computers.

Released in the United States last fall, all have programmes that store phone numbers, addresses and schedules. Windows CE lets them transfer the data automatically to desktop PCs and updates both computers with any changes.

While European roll-outs for the more consumer-oriented Cassiopeia are not yet set, the HP and Philips now have ready English-language versions of their palmtops, which are aimed at business users. German, French and other models due later this year, they said.
"The Velo is for the on-the-go professional, the person who needs to access data for his job and needs to communicate," Miriam Vriens, Philips product manager, told Reuters.
"A lot of people use a laptop to do that now, but a laptop is heavy and it takes time to open up and set up," she said.

The Velo and the OmniGo cost about $1,000, at least half of a laptop price. They also fit in a jacket pocket, turn on instantly, run for 20 or more hours on AA batteries and can connect to a mobile phone to download or send email messages.
Unlike Apple Computer Inc.'s Newton "personal digital assistant", which debuted at CeBIT three years ago and flopped, the Windows CE handhelds do not read "pen-input."
Instead of writing notes on the screen and having the computer turn it into text, users of Windows CE devices have to make do with tiny keyboards.
But these products have the advantage of Microsoft's support, Vriens said.
"There are more than 3,000 companies developing software for Windows CE, so that tells you people will be able to do a lot of things with these products very soon," she said.

"The Newton was perhaps too early," said Andreas Barth, European chief of Compaq Computer Corp., which gave limited demonstrations of its Windows CE machine, the PC Companion 120. "But now the Internet is taking off, so there's a lot more data these machines can access."

Psion Plc aimed to capitalise on the Internet trend with its Psion 3 palmtop, which does not use Windows CE. At CBIT, Psion showed its machine accessing World Wide Web pages and sending faxes via a separate mobile phone.

Sharp Corp's Color ZR, the only one of the palmtops with a colour screen, went in another direction. Hooked up to a digital camera, it showed the user his photographs instantly. The camera/ZR package would cost about $1,500.
Apple also showed a new Newton, while U.S. Robotics and Fujitsu Personal Systems Inc. showed other handheld computers.
